The result is a table with the columns id, source, target, and rel: one row per edge sorted by id, with endpoints given as node ids and rel empty (null)." width="100%"} Returns all edges with a consistent column structure: - column 1: `id` (i64, mandatory, sorted ascending) - column 2: `source` (i64, mandatory) - column 3: `target` (i64, mandatory) - column 4: `rel` (str, mandatory, null if not set) - columns 5-N: Other attributes (alphabetically sorted) - weight is included as a special attribute if present The DataFrame is always sorted by edge ID in ascending order. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [labels]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, the `source` and `target` columns hold the endpoints' labels (a node without a label shows its ID as a string) instead of their node IDs, which makes the table easier to read. Defaults to `False`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [pl.DataFrame]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A Polars DataFrame with edges sorted by `id`. If the graph has no edges, the frame has no rows but still has the `id`, `source`, `target` and `rel` columns (and `weight` on a weighted graph). ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The layout mirrors `get_node_df()` in spirit: `id`, `source`, `target`, and `rel` always come first (in that order), followed by `weight` and any other custom edge attributes in alphabetical order, with rows sorted by `id` ascending. `weight` is treated as a first-class attribute column rather than a bare number so it can be filtered and aggregated with the rest of the schema. Missing `rel` values appear as `None`. Attributes whose values differ in type from edge to edge are reconciled as in `get_node_df()`. The `id`, `source` and `target` columns always hold the edge IDs and endpoints, so an attribute with one of those names is left out of the table, and so is a `weight` attribute when any edge has a weight (`get_edge_attrs()` reads them). ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~get_node_df`) : The nodes as a Polars DataFrame, for joining to the edges. [](`~get_edge_attrs`) : One edge attribute as a dictionary keyed by edge ID. [](`~get_edges_as_tuples`) : The edges as plain (id, source, target) tuples. ## Examples {.doc-examples} The frame has a row per edge, sorted by ID. `id`, `source`, `target` and `rel` come first, then `weight` and the other edge attributes. `labels=True` gives the endpoints by label: ::: {#9f2b7389 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) graph.add_edges( [ ("A", "B", 1.5, {"rel": "friend"}), ("B", "C", 2.0, {"rel": "colleague"}), ] ) graph.get_edge_df(labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ### Ties across the split Zachary's karate club split in two after a dispute between its instructor (member 0) and its administrator (member 33), and the `faction` attribute records which side each member joined. Joining each end of each edge to its faction finds the ties that cross the split: ::: {#78da766d .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import polars as pl karate = ec.karate_club() sides = karate.get_node_df().select("label", "faction") source_sides = sides.rename({"label": "source", "faction": "from"}) target_sides = sides.rename({"label": "target", "faction": "to"}) edges = ( karate.get_edge_df(labels=True) .join(source_sides, on="source") .join(target_sides, on="target") ) crossing = edges.filter(pl.col("from") != pl.col("to")) crossing.select("source", "target", "from", "to") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
